title: How Ancient Humans Survived in Prehistory?
text:
🔥 Go deeper with the full course: https://ancient-minds-academy1.teachable.com/p/the-secret-lives-of-ancient-humans
The Secret Lives of Ancient Humans — 10 modules, 3.5+ hours of exclusive content.

Before cities, before farming, before written history — how did our ancient ancestors actually survive? In this video, we explore the remarkable world of prehistoric human survival: the tools they made, the food they hunted, the shelters they built, and the instincts that kept our species alive for hundreds of thousands of years.
From the ice age to the first fires, from cave dwellings to early social structures — this is the raw, unfiltered story of human resilience at its most primal.
🔑 What you'll learn:
✅ How early humans hunted, gathered, and found food
✅ What shelters and tools prehistoric people actually used
✅ The social structures and survival instincts that shaped humanity
✅ How our ancestors adapted to extreme environments and climate shifts
💡 We take modern survival for granted — but the story of how humans made it this far is one of the most extraordinary tales ever told. Don't miss it.

Imagine waking up tomorrow. No phone, no
grocery store, no running water, no
heating. Just you, a forest, and
approximately 10,000 things that want to
kill you. That's Tuesday for our
ancestors. We talk a lot about ancient
civilizations. Rome, Egypt, Greece, but
those guys already had it figured out.
Bread, wine, slaves to do the laundry.
Comfortable. What I want to talk about
today goes much further back, way
further. We're talking about the people
who had nothing. No agriculture, no
cities, no concept of a week end. Just
raw, brutal, beautiful survival. And
somehow, they pulled it off for hundreds
of thousands of years. So, today, we're
diving deep into how prehistoric humans
actually survived. Not the sanitized
museum exhibit version, the real thing.
The fire, the fear, the weird food, the
social drama, and the absolutely insane
mental fortitude it took just to make it
to age 30. Let's go. Before we give
credit to our ancestors, let's be honest
about one thing. If you or I were
dropped into the Paleolithic era right
now, we would be dead within a week.
Probably day three, honestly. You don't
know which berries are poisonous. You
don't know how to start a fire without a
lighter. You can't track an animal. You
can't build a shelter. You can't even
read the weather properly. You'd
probably drink bad water on day one,
spend day two with catastrophic stomach
issues behind a bush, and by day three,
a cave bear would smell you from half a
mile away, and that would be that. Game
over. But, here's the fascinating thing.
Our ancestors weren't born knowing this
stuff, either. They learned it. Across
generations, slowly, painfully, through
a lot of trial and error. And by error,
I mean death. A lot of death. The human
species is essentially the result of
millions of years of people figuring out
what not to do. Every piece of survival
knowledge that made it to the next
generation was paid for in blood,
hunger, and probably a lot of frustrated
grunting. So, let's break down exactly
how they did it. Here's something nobody
tells you about prehistoric life.
Ancient humans thought about food
approximately 90% of the time. The other
10% was split between sleeping,
reproducing, and panicking about
predators. And honestly, fair. Finding
food in the Paleolithic era was not like
opening your fridge at midnight. It was
a full-time job with no salary, no
guaranteed outcome, and a real
possibility that the food would try to
kill you before you killed it. Hunting
was the glamorous part, the stuff we put
in paintings. Big mammoths, giant bison,
woolly rhinos. But let's be real, most
of the time early humans weren't hunting
mammoths. You know why? Because a
mammoth is roughly the size of a school
bus and has tusks the length of a sedan.
Early humans with sharpened sticks had
to be extremely creative, extremely
patient, and extremely lucky to take one
down. What they actually ate most of the
time was smaller game. Rabbits, birds,
fish, insects. Yes, insects. Packed with
protein, easy to catch, delicious if
you're hungry enough, which they always
were. If you're making a face right now,
remember that half the world still eats
insects today and considers them a
delicacy. You're the weird one. But
hunting, even small game, was only part
of the equation. The real unsung hero of
prehistoric nutrition was gathering.
Women in most hunter-gatherer societies
were responsible for gathering, and
studies suggest they actually provided
the majority of the group's caloric
intake. Roots, tubers, nuts, seeds,
fruits, berries, mushrooms, leaves. They
knew the landscape like a map. They knew
which plants were safe, which were
seasonal, which could be stored, which
could be used medicinally. This was not
casual knowledge. This was encyclopedic,
generational, deeply sophisticated
botanical expertise. A prehistoric woman
identifying which mushroom was edible
versus which one would make your organs
shut down was performing a cognitive
task that would genuinely impress a
modern biologist. And then, there was
the truly underrated technique,
scavenging. We used to think scavenging
was what you did when you failed at
hunting, the loser option. New research
suggests it was actually a deliberate,
skilled strategy. Early humans would
follow predators, lions, hyenas, observe
a kill, then use noise, numbers, and
fire to chase the predator off and steal
the carcass. Bold? Absolutely.
Effective? Extremely. Safe? Debatable.
The point is, prehistoric humans were
not picky. They ate what was available,
they learned what was safe, and they
developed a nutritional flexibility that
is genuinely remarkable. A modern human
raised on processed food would have the
dietary resilience of a tissue in a
rainstorm. Our ancestors could eat
almost anything, almost anywhere. Let's
talk about where these people slept. The
word cave comes up a lot when we talk
about prehistoric humans. Cavemen, cave
paintings, cave bears. And yes, caves
were used, but here's the thing. Caves
are actually pretty great real estate if
you think about it. Stable temperature
year-round, protection from wind and
rain, defensible entrance, natural
structure that requires zero
construction. The problem? There aren't
that many caves, and the ones that exist
were often already occupied by animals
who are significantly larger and angrier
than any human. So, our ancestors also
built shelters, and this is where things
get genuinely impressive. Archaeological
evidence, some of it over 400,000 years
old, shows early humans constructing
shelters from branches, animal hides,
bones, and mammoth tusks. They were
building architecture before they had a
written language, before they had metal
tools, before they had anything we'd
recognize as technology. The
construction logic was sound. Angle
branches against each other to form a
frame, layer hides over the top for
waterproofing, weigh down the edges with
rocks or bones to keep wind from ripping
everything apart. Inside, line the floor
with dry grass or more hides for
insulation. Result? A structure that's
warm, relatively dry, and invisible to
aerial predators. Not bad for someone
who invented it from scratch with no
YouTube tutorial. And here's a detail
that I love. Evidence suggests
prehistoric humans were intensely aware
of wind direction when placing their
shelters. They positioned entrances away
from prevailing winds. They built near
water, but not too near. Close enough
for convenience, far enough to avoid
flooding and the predators that gathered
at water sources at night. These weren't
random choices. This was environmental
literacy at a profound level. They were
reading the landscape and making
calculated decisions based on patterns
they'd observed over years. That's not
instinct. That's intelligence. Then came
the best invention of all time, fire.
Fire is the greatest invention in human
history and nothing else comes close.
Not the wheel, not the internet, not
antibiotics.
Fire. Here's why. Before controlled
fire, humans were basically just
slightly smarter apes. With fire,
everything changed all at once. Cooking
transformed nutrition. Raw meat is hard
to chew, hard to digest, and often full
of parasites that will absolutely ruin
your month. Cooked meat is tender,
easier to digest, and vastly safer. The
caloric extraction from cooked food
versus raw food is dramatically higher.
Some researchers argue that cooking
literally accelerated human brain
development because we were suddenly
getting more energy from the same food,
and that extra energy went straight to
fueling our expanding brains. So, in a
very real sense, fire made us smarter.
We cooked ourselves into intelligence.
Warmth extended the range of
environments humans could survive.
Before fire, you basically had to live
somewhere temperate. With fire, you
could push into colder climates, higher
altitudes. You could survive winter. Ice
Age Europe became habitable. Siberia
became crossable. The entire
colonization of the planet by Homo
sapiens was enabled in large part by our
ability to carry warmth with us. Light
extended the productive day. After dark,
without fire, you do nothing. You sit in
the dark and hope nothing eats you. With
fire, you can work, talk, make tools,
plan, socialize. Firelight extended
human cognitive and social activity by
hours every day. Protection kept
predators away. Most animals are
terrified of fire. A fire burning at the
entrance of your shelter means wolves,
lions, and hyenas keep their distance.
It's an alarm system and offense rolled
into one. And then there's the social
dimension, the campfire. Humans sitting
around a fire together, sharing food,
telling stories. This is where human
culture was born. Oral tradition,
mythology, social bonds, all of it
incubated around a fire. Some
anthropologists call it the first
technology of community. How did they
make it? Multiple methods, depending on
era and location. Striking flint against
iron pyrite creates sparks. And if those
sparks land on dry tender, fungus, fine
bark fibers, dry grass, you've got fire.
Friction methods, a wooden stick rotated
rapidly against a flat board, also work,
though they require technique and
stamina. Both methods were known and
used by prehistoric humans, and both
require far more skill than they look
like they do. Try it sometime. I dare
you. Come back and tell me how long it
took. Then, there is the single most
important survival truth of the
prehistoric world. You could not survive
alone. This cannot be overstated. A lone
human in the Paleolithic was a dead
human. Too slow, too weak, too
vulnerable, no claws, no venom, no
shell, no camouflage. Humans,
biologically speaking, are laughably
unimpressive as individual organisms.
But as a group, terrifying.
Hunter-gatherer bands typically numbered
between 20 and 50 people. This was not
random. This was the optimal size for
survival. Large enough to share the
cognitive load of survival knowledge,
coordinate hunts, and defend against
predators. Small enough to be fed by the
local environment without depleting it.
Within these groups, roles were not
rigid, but they were real. Experienced
hunters shared knowledge with the young.
Elders who could no longer run were
invaluable repositories of environmental
memory. They remembered the drought of
40 years ago, the migration pattern that
only happened every decade, the plant
that grew after wildfires. Their
knowledge could save the group. Children
were collective responsibility. Everyone
helped raise them. The concept of it
takes a village isn't a metaphor. It was
literal survival policy. Conflict within
the group was genuinely dangerous
because a fractured group was a dead
group. This created intense social
pressure toward cooperation, toward
fairness, toward reading other people's
emotions and intentions accurately. Some
researchers argued that the complexity
of human social life, the gossip, the
politics, the emotional intelligence,
was the primary driver of human brain
expansion. We got smart not to build
tools, but to manage each other. The
interpersonal drama of prehistoric life
was probably spectacular by the way. 50
people, extremely stressed, living in
each other's pockets 24 hours a day, no
privacy, scarce resources, and genuine
mortal stakes. If that's not a reality
show waiting to happen, I don't know
what is. But there's still another
problem. You get a cut today. You clean
it, put a bandage on it, maybe some
antibiotic cream. Done. You have a
fever, you drink water, take some
ibuprofen, sleep it off. In prehistory,
an infected cut could kill you. A bad
fever could kill you. A broken bone
could kill you. Childbirth regularly
killed women. Tooth decay was genuinely
life-threatening, and yet people
survived, even to old age sometimes.
How? Herbal medicine, first of all, was
far more developed than we tend to
assume. Archaeological evidence shows
prehistoric humans using plants
medicinally. Yarrow for wound treatment,
willow bark, which contains salicylic
acid, the active ingredient in aspirin,
for pain and fever. Ephedra as a
stimulant. Various plants with genuine
antimicrobial properties were applied to
wounds. This wasn't magic. This was
empirical medicine. Try this plant on
this wound. Does it get better or worse?
Remember the answer. Tell your children.
That's the scientific method, just at a
slower pace and with higher stakes for
being wrong. Wound management included
cleaning, packing with certain clays or
mosses, and using animal fat as a
barrier. Were these as effective as
modern medicine? No, but they were
something, and sometimes something is
the difference between life and death.
Bone healing evidence is genuinely
moving. Skeletal remains from the
Paleolithic show healed fractures,
complex ones that would have required
weeks of immobility. This means the
injured person was fed and cared for by
the group while they couldn't
contribute. It means cooperation,
compassion, and social investment in
individual members who couldn't pull
their weight temporarily. That is not
primitive behavior. That is civilization
in its most essential form. We've talked
a lot about physical survival, but let's
take a moment for the psychological
dimension because I think it's wildly
under appreciated. Imagine the baseline
stress level of prehistoric life. Every
single day you face the real possibility
of starvation, of predator attack, of
illness, of injury, of losing someone
you love to any of the above. There is
no safety net, no insurance, no doctor
on call. That is an immense
psychological load. And yet, the
evidence suggests prehistoric humans
were not crushed by it. They created
art. They buried their dead with
ceremony. They decorated their bodies.
They made music. They told stories so
complex and meaningful that those
stories shaped entire future cultures.
They had a relationship with joy despite
living in conditions that would send
most modern humans into a full
psychological breakdown by the end of
week one. How? Partly, community. Being
surrounded by people you trust, who
depend on you and on whom you depend, is
one of the most powerful psychological
stabilizers known to humans even today.
Depression and anxiety are strongly
correlated with social isolation.
Prehistoric humans were almost never
socially isolated. Partly, purpose.
Every single day had clear, meaningful
tasks. Find food, maintain shelter, care
for children. There's no existential
void when you have a genuine survival
level reason to get up in the morning.
And partly, and this is the bit that I
find most fascinating, they had ritual,
ceremony, burial rites, seasonal
celebrations, rites of passage. These
weren't just superstition. Ritual is a
technology for managing the
psychological weight of uncertainty.
When you don't know why things happen,
ritual gives you the feeling, however
illusory, of agency. And that feeling of
agency is psychologically protective. We
still use it today. We just call it
different things. But the question
everyone's asking is how our ancestors
managed to survive for hundreds of
thousands of years without Chat GPT? No,
seriously, how did they manage to
survive for so long? People with our
exact same brains and bodies have
existed for at least 300,000 years,
possibly longer, and our genus, Homo,
goes back nearly 3 million years. For
the overwhelming majority of human
existence, people lived the way we've
been describing today, hunting,
gathering, sheltering, cooperating,
adapting, generation after generation
after generation across ice ages,
droughts, volcanic winters, continental
migrations. They didn't just survive,
they dominated. By the time the ice
retreated and agriculture became
possible, humans were present on every
continent except Antarctica. They had
crossed land bridges into the Americas.
They had navigated open ocean to reach
Australia. They had lived through the
Toba super volcano, possibly the closest
our species ever came to extinction, and
rebuilt from what may have been a few
thousand surviving individuals. That is
not luck. That is an extraordinary,
almost incomprehensible resilience. So,
from now on, when your pizza is
delivered 5 minutes late, and you yell
at the delivery man, remember that
somewhere on Earth, 69,000 years ago,
your great, great, great, great, great,
great, great, great, great, great
grandfather had to fight a huge 700 kg
cave bear just to decide whose cave it
was.
